title: Occasion and publication
short: Written at Nether Stowey, Somerset, in February 1798; first printed in 1798 in a quarto with 'Fears in Solitude' and 'France: An Ode'.
body: Coleridge was living in a cottage at Nether Stowey with his wife Sara and their son Hartley, then about seventeen months old; Wordsworth and Dorothy were nearby at Alfoxden. The poem was published by Joseph Johnson in 1798 and revised several times (in the Poetical Register of 1808-9 and in the collected editions of 1828 and 1829), the six-line ending of 1798 being dropped by 1829. The archive text is the revised version, which ends at 'the quiet Moon'. It is the most admired of the 'conversation poems', blank-verse meditations in a familiar voice addressed to a listener, here a sleeping infant.

title: secret ministry
short: Frost works invisibly and silently, like a priest's or servant's ministry: a hidden, beneficent agency in nature.
body: 'Ministry' means service, and in a religious sense the office of a minister; Coleridge was himself a Unitarian preacher at this period. The phrase gives the frost a purpose without a visible agent, and the poem's theology of a God who 'teaches' through nature is already implied. The phrase returns in the final sentence, making the poem circular. Hoar-frost forms best on still, clear nights, which is why the next line adds 'Unhelped by any wind'.

title: The owlet's cry
short: The only sound breaks the silence twice, intensifying the stillness.
body: 'Owlet' is a young or small owl, and in literary usage simply an owl. The repetition ('and hark, again! loud as before') makes the reader listen, while the frost's 'secret ministry' is soundless. The interjection gives the opening the feel of a live, present-tense meditation. Owls recur in Coleridge's poems of this period ('Christabel' opens at midnight with the owl's cry), and their calls serve as markers of night and solitude.

title: inmates
short: The people living in the cottage: wife, child and guests (not prisoners).
body: In older usage an 'inmate' is one who lives in a house with others, a lodger or member of the household. The word is neutral here, but it makes the cottage a small community from which the speaker is isolated by wakefulness. The household was not small: besides his wife and son, Coleridge often had guests at Nether Stowey, and in early 1798 Wordsworth and Dorothy were frequent visitors from nearby Alfoxden. The isolation is the chosen solitude of the late night, not loneliness.

title: Abstruser musings
short: More recondite, difficult thoughts: Coleridge's metaphysical speculation.
body: 'Abstruse' (Latin abstrusus, 'hidden, concealed') means hard to understand. The comparative suggests that solitude suits such thoughts; but the poem actually moves away from abstraction into memory and hope for the child. The phrase is often taken as self-mocking, given Coleridge's reputation for metaphysics. Coleridge's reading in 1797-98 included Hartley, Berkeley, Spinoza and the Neoplatonists, and in September 1798 he left for Germany, partly to study philosophy.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'abstruse'

title: My cradled infant
short: Hartley Coleridge (1796-1849), born 19 September 1796, about seventeen months old when the poem was written.
body: Hartley was named after the philosopher David Hartley, whose associationist psychology Coleridge then admired. The father's hopes for him in this poem have often been set against Hartley's later life: he became a gifted but troubled poet who lived in the Lake District, where the poem imagines him wandering. Wordsworth's 'To H. C., Six Years Old' is also addressed to him.

title: so calm, that it disturbs ... extreme silentness
short: A paradox: the calm is so complete that it unsettles thought.
body: The silence 'vexes meditation' because there is nothing to resist or respond to; the mind turns inward. 'Silentness' is an uncommon variant of 'silence'. The next lines try to fill the silence with a list of what is present but unheard: 'Sea, hill, and wood ... With all the numberless goings-on of life, / Inaudible as dreams!' The repeated phrase 'Sea, and hill, and wood' sounds like an incantation against the quiet.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'silentness'

title: This populous village!
short: Nether Stowey is full of life, yet all is silent as dreams.
body: The paradox of a 'populous' place that makes no sound continues the poem's play on presence and absence. The phrase may echo Milton's simile of Satan in Eden 'As one who long in populous city pent' (Paradise Lost 9.445), which Coleridge recalls more explicitly later in the poem ('In the great city, pent'). The exclamations imitate the movement of a mind registering its surroundings, a hallmark of the conversation-poem manner.

title: Only that film ... the sole unquiet thing
short: A flake of soot fluttering on the grate; Coleridge's note says such films are called 'strangers' and foretell a visitor.
body: Coleridge's note (1798) explains that 'in all parts of the kingdom these films are called strangers' and are supposed to portend the arrival of some absent friend. Cowper's The Task, Book 4 ('The Winter Evening'), has a passage on the 'sooty films' on the bars of the grate and the superstition they prompt, which Coleridge's poem seems to recall. The film is the only moving thing in a still world, and it becomes the link to memory in the next paragraph.

title: a companionable form
short: The mind, alone, makes the fluttering film into a companion with 'dim sympathies'.
body: The film seems to share the speaker's restlessness. 'Freaks' are whims or capricious movements; 'puny flaps' its small motions. Coleridge is analysing how a solitary mind projects its own moods onto objects, a process the next lines describe. The lines anticipate a theme central to Coleridge's later criticism, the difference between a fancy that merely plays with images and an imagination that finds true relation between mind and world.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'freak'

anchor: Echo or mirror seeking of itself
title: Echo or mirror seeking of itself, / And makes a toy of Thought
short: Revised wording (1828-29): the idle mind looks everywhere for its own echo or reflection.
body: These lines replace a longer passage of 1798, which spoke of 'Idle thought' and 'fantastic playfulness'; the passage was reworked in 1808-9 and again in 1828. The final text compresses the idea: the mind finds itself everywhere and trivialises thought into a toy. Critics read the lines as Coleridge's critique of solipsistic fancy, set against the poem's later vision of nature as God's language, in which the mind receives meaning rather than projecting it.

title: Structure: the 'greater Romantic lyric'
short: The poem moves out from the present scene into memory and then to the future and back: a circular blank-verse meditation.
body: M. H. Abrams took this poem as a model of what he called the 'greater Romantic lyric': a speaker in a particular outdoor or domestic setting, whose meditation moves from the scene into memory and feeling and returns to the scene with a new understanding. The half-line indent at 'But O! how oft' marks the turn into the past. The verse is blank verse with a conversational, flexible syntax.

title: at school ... the bars
short: Christ's Hospital, the London charity school which Coleridge attended from 1782 to 1791.
body: After his father's death in 1781, Coleridge was sent to Christ's Hospital in the City of London. 'The bars' are the bars of the schoolroom grate where, as a boy, he watched for the same fluttering 'stranger'. 'Presageful' means full of foreboding or prediction. Charles Lamb, a schoolfellow, described Coleridge at school in his essays. Coleridge's memories of the school, its discipline and its loneliness for a country boy, recur in his letters and in Biographia Literaria.

sources.cite: Richard Holmes, Coleridge: Early Visions (London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1989)
S. T. Coleridge, Biographia Literaria (1817), ch. 1, on the Rev. James Bowyer of Christ's Hospital (Project Gutenberg text)

title: my sweet birth-place, and the old church-tower
short: Ottery St Mary in Devon, where Coleridge's father was vicar and master of the grammar school.
body: The church of St Mary at Ottery, with its tall towers, dominated the small town; the boy at school dreamed of its bells ringing for the annual fair. 'Fair-day' is the day of the town fair. The bells as 'the poor man's only music' is a characteristic sympathetic touch. The memory of the fair and its bells is a memory within a memory: the boy at school is remembering an earlier childhood at home. The layered time-scheme is one of the poem's most admired features.

sources.cite: Richard Holmes, Coleridge: Early Visions (London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1989)

anchor: articulate sounds of things to come
title: Most like articulate sounds of things to come
short: The bells seem to speak, prophesying the future: a first version of the poem's theme of nature as language.
body: 'Articulate' means jointed into distinct words. The child hears meaning in the bells, as the boy at school reads meaning into the soot-film. The theme comes to its fullest form in the paragraph promising the infant 'that eternal language' of nature. The phrase also anticipates the boy's hope of a visitor: the bells seem to promise future happenings, as the soot-film promises a 'stranger'. The child's imagination is always reaching toward what is to come.

sources.cite: M. H. Abrams, 'Structure and Style in the Greater Romantic Lyric', in From Sensibility to Romanticism, ed. F. W. Hilles and H. Bloom (New York: Oxford UP, 1965)
J. C. C. Mays, ed., Poetical Works, The Collected Works of Samuel Taylor Coleridge 16 (Princeton UP, 2001), 'Frost at Midnight'

title: the stern preceptor
short: The Rev. James Bowyer (or Boyer), head master at Christ's Hospital, famous for severity.
body: In chapter 1 of Biographia Literaria Coleridge credits 'the Reverend James Bowyer' with training his taste and also remembers his discipline. 'Preceptor' means teacher. 'My swimming book' is the page blurring before eyes that are only pretending to study. Charles Lamb's essays on Christ's Hospital also remember Bowyer's severity. The memory of fear in the classroom sets up the contrast with the freedom imagined for Hartley.

sources.cite: S. T. Coleridge, Biographia Literaria (1817), ch. 1, on the Rev. James Bowyer of Christ's Hospital (Project Gutenberg text)
Richard Holmes, Coleridge: Early Visions (London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1989)

title: the stranger's face ... sister more beloved
short: The boy hoped the 'stranger' would be a visitor from home: a townsman, an aunt, or his sister.
body: The superstition becomes a child's longing. The sister is probably Ann (Nancy) Coleridge, who died in 1791. The 1829 text italicised 'stranger', stressing the link with the soot-film's folk name. The repeated hope ('still my heart leaped up, / For still I hoped') shows how intensely the lonely schoolboy longed for home. The sister's death gives the memory a retrospective sadness that the poem does not spell out.

title: when we both were clothed alike
short: Small boys and girls were dressed alike in frocks or petticoats until boys were 'breeched' at four to seven.
body: The phrase identifies the sister as his playmate in early childhood, before boys were put into breeches. The detail is affectionate and exact, and it marks how far back the memory reaches. Coleridge was the youngest of a large family, and the 'sister more beloved' of the line was a companion of his early childhood in Ottery.

sources.cite: Richard Holmes, Coleridge: Early Visions (London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1989)

title: Dear Babe ... interspersed vacancies
short: The poem turns to the sleeping child, whose breathing fills the gaps in the father's thought.
body: 'Interspersed vacancies' are the pauses scattered through thought; the child's breathing fills them as the film did. The address to a silent listener is typical of the conversation poems (compare 'This Lime-Tree Bower my Prison', addressed to Charles Lamb). The stillness of the sleeping child is the counterpart of the silent frost; both are presences that do not speak but fill the poet's attention.

sources.cite: M. H. Abrams, 'Structure and Style in the Greater Romantic Lyric', in From Sensibility to Romanticism, ed. F. W. Hilles and H. Bloom (New York: Oxford UP, 1965)
S. T. Coleridge, 'This Lime-Tree Bower my Prison' (1797; pub. 1800), in E. H. Coleridge, ed., Complete Poetical Works (1912)

title: In the great city, pent 'mid cloisters dim
short: Echoes Milton's 'As one who long in populous city pent' (Paradise Lost 9.445) and Coleridge's own 'This Lime-Tree Bower'.
body: 'Pent' means confined. Milton's simile describes Satan's delight in Eden as like a city-dweller's in the country air. Coleridge had already used the phrase of Lamb, 'In the great City pent', in 'This Lime-Tree Bower my Prison' (1797). The 'cloisters dim' are those of Christ's Hospital, on the site of a former Franciscan friary. The contrast of city and country education is an eighteenth- and Romantic-period commonplace.

Richard Holmes, Coleridge: Early Visions (London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1989)

title: shalt wander like a breeze
short: The father's wish that his son grow up free in mountain country, by lakes and crags.
body: The landscape is not Somerset but the Lake District or some ideal upland; the Coleridges moved to Keswick in 1800, and Hartley did grow up among lakes and mountains. The clouds that 'image' (reflect, mirror) the lakes and crags make nature a set of mutual reflections, a contrast to the self-reflecting mind of the first paragraph. The breeze is a key Romantic image of free, unforced inspiration (compare Coleridge's 'The Eolian Harp').

sources.cite: Richard Holmes, Coleridge: Early Visions (London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1989)
J. C. C. Mays, ed., Poetical Works, The Collected Works of Samuel Taylor Coleridge 16 (Princeton UP, 2001), 'Frost at Midnight'

title: that eternal language, which thy God / Utters
short: Nature as God's language, an idea from Berkeley, whom Coleridge then admired (he named his second son Berkeley in 1798).
body: Berkeley argued that what we see is a set of signs by which God speaks to us, 'the universal language of the Author of nature' (New Theory of Vision; Alciphron). Coleridge adapts the idea: the 'lovely shapes and sounds intelligible' are words of a divine language through which the child will learn. 'Intelligible' means capable of being understood, perhaps with a philosophical sense of what is grasped by the intellect.

M. H. Abrams, 'Structure and Style in the Greater Romantic Lyric', in From Sensibility to Romanticism, ed. F. W. Hilles and H. Bloom (New York: Oxford UP, 1965)

title: Himself in all, and all things in himself
short: God teaches himself in all things, and all things in himself: a Neoplatonic, near-pantheist formula.
body: The line describes a God who is present in everything and contains everything. Coleridge in 1798 was still a Unitarian with pantheist sympathies; he later worried about pantheism. 'By giving make it ask' says that God's gifts awaken a desire for more, so that the child's spirit learns to seek. The formula is close to Paul's 'in him we live, and move, and have our being' (Acts 17:28), which Coleridge as a preacher knew well, and to Neoplatonic ideas of a world that comes from and returns to the One.

title: the redbreast sit and sing
short: The robin, which sings in winter, and the smoking thatch of a thaw: a catalogue of seasons all made 'sweet'.
body: The final paragraph moves from summer to winter details: a robin among snow tufts on a mossy apple-tree, the thatch steaming in a sun-thaw, the eave-drops heard only in the pauses ('trances') of the wind. The precise rural observation answers the earlier promise that the child will learn from nature. 'The general earth' means the whole earth, the earth at large. The details are all small and domestic, a deliberate scaling down from the grand 'eternal language' of the previous paragraph.

anchor: Quietly shining to the quiet Moon
title: The ending
short: The poem returns to frost, icicles and moonlight, closing the circle begun with 'secret ministry'.
body: The original 1798 version continued for six more lines, imagining the baby stretching towards the icicles; Coleridge later explained that he omitted them because they destroyed the poem's return upon itself, and the cut stands in the 1829 text. The present ending fixes the poem in stillness: the eave-drops, frozen by 'the secret ministry of frost', shine 'quietly' to the 'quiet Moon'. Abrams treats the return to the opening scene, changed by the meditation, as the defining move of the greater Romantic lyric.
